title: Year three close: the people and their story
hookLine: from Joshua's river to today, one long story
tomorrow: Year four opens: how it all works

lines: WHAT MEAN YE BY THESE STONES?
cards: Back near the start of this year, the people crossed the Jordan, and Joshua set up stones on the far bank.

Not to be admired: to be asked about, so that someday the children would say, "What mean ye by these stones?" and someone would have to tell the story. Now the same question can be put to the whole year.
What were all those days for? Kings and prophets, poems and exiles, rabbis and refugees, a language woken up, a people still singing. Today, one answer, told as one story.

teach.h: THE FORMER PROPHETS: A RIVER, KINGS.
teach.b: Here's the year, as that answer. First, the Former Prophets. The day Moses died, the story didn't stop.
Joshua crossed the river, the judges rose and fell, Samuel anointed kings, and the kingdom split and fell.
Second, the Latter Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve, voices that warned before the fall and comforted after it, down to Ezekiel's dry bones standing up again.

teach.h: THE WRITINGS, THEN AFTER THE BIBLE.
teach.b: Third, the Writings: Ruth choosing a people, Job arguing with heaven, Esther finding her voice, Lamentations weeping over the city, Ezra and Nehemiah coming home to rebuild.
Then the Bible's last page turned, and the story kept going. The Maccabees and Rome. Yavneh and the Talmud.
Babylon and Baghdad, Spain and the Rhineland, Safed and the villages of the east. The Americas, the return of Hebrew, the Shoah, and after.

teach.h: A QUESTION WAITING FOR THE NEXT CHILD.
teach.b: Women whose names were nearly lost. And Jewish life today, with its food and music and arguments and candles. That's the year: not a list of dates, but one long thread, picked up by each generation and handed on.
And notice where the Tanakh itself chooses to stop.

The Torah ends on the bank of the Jordan, the land in sight and the crossing still ahead. The Prophets open with the command to cross. So the stones on the bank were never a monument to a finished event.
They were a question waiting for the next child.

how: Jews say the Shehecheyanu blessing at the start of festivals, on first times and at milestones, and they retell their history in the cycle of festivals and fasts, from Passover to Tisha b'Av to Hanukkah.

o: the mourner's prayer said for a parent who has died
the blessing said over wine at the Shabbat table
who has kept us alive: a blessing for new seasons

p: a river crossing, judges and kings
warning before the fall, comfort after

s: the stones by the Jordan were set up as a monument to be admired
they were set up to be asked about: what mean ye by these stones?
the Torah ends with the people on the bank of the Jordan, before the crossing
the land is in sight and the crossing is still ahead. the Prophets open with the command to cross.
Jewish history ends where the Bible ends
the Bible's last page turned and the story kept going: Rome, Yavneh, Babylon, Spain, the Americas, today.

games.q: you're a parent by the Jordan, years after the crossing. your child points at the pile of stones and asks, what mean ye by these stones? what do you do?
o: tell the story of the crossing.
tell them to ask the priests.
games.why: the book of Joshua says the stones exist for exactly this: when the children ask, you tell them the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark.

practice: Let the year pass in front of you: one story that stayed with you, one person, one line.
When Jews reach a new season or a milestone, they say the Shehecheyanu, which blesses God, who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season.

If you pray, say it now, in Hebrew or in English, for the year you've just walked; if you don't, simply sit with the thought that you've arrived at the end of a long story and the start of its next part.

wordCard.voice: Shehecheyanu. Hebrew for who has kept us alive: the blessing for milestones, fitting for a year that carried the people's whole story to the river's edge and beyond. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: who has kept us alive, the key word of the blessing for new seasons and milestones.

carryVoice: Your line: the story goes on. Tomorrow, year four, and how it all works. Year three, complete.
